nameStory: The Blue Button gets its charming name from its distinctive appearance - it looks exactly like a small, bright blue button that might have fallen off a sailor's coat and floated out to sea. The circular, flat shape with its brilliant blue coloration makes it one of the most aptly named creatures in the ocean.
description: The Blue Button is a fascinating marine colony that looks like a small, translucent blue disc floating on the ocean's surface. Though it resembles a jellyfish, it's actually a colony of tiny interconnected animals called hydroids working together as one unit. These coin-sized creatures typically measure about an inch across and drift with ocean currents, occasionally washing up on New England beaches after storms.

idTips.label: Circular blue disc
idTips.description: Perfectly round, flat body with a brilliant blue color and translucent, almost glass-like appearance that catches the light

idTips.label: Central gas-filled float
idTips.description: Hard, button-like center that feels slightly firm to the touch and helps the colony stay afloat at the surface

idTips.label: Radiating tentacles
idTips.description: Short, thread-like tentacles extending from the edges that may feel slightly sticky and can cause mild skin irritation

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: About the size of a quarter or half-dollar, with a smooth, gel-like texture that's firmer than a typical jellyfish

idTips.label: Beach-cast appearance
idTips.description: When washed ashore, often appears deflated and less vibrant but retains the distinctive blue coloration and circular shape

habitat: Blue Buttons are occasionally found washed up on New England's sandy beaches, particularly after strong onshore winds or storms that blow them in from warmer offshore waters. They're most commonly spotted on exposed ocean beaches from Cape Cod to Maine during late summer and early fall. Look for them in the wrack line among other storm-tossed marine debris.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in New England waters as ocean temperatures are still too cold for these warm-water visitors.
seasonality.summer: Occasional sightings begin in late summer when Gulf Stream waters and warm weather patterns can carry them northward to our coastal waters.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for Blue Button strandings on New England beaches, especially after tropical storms or hurricanes push warm water masses northward.
seasonality.winter: Not found in New England waters during winter months due to cold temperatures.

funFact: Despite looking like a single animal, each Blue Button is actually a floating city of hundreds of tiny specialized creatures - some dedicated to feeding, others to reproduction, and others to defense - all working together so perfectly they function as one organism.
confusionNotes: Blue Buttons are sometimes confused with small jellyfish, but they're much firmer to the touch, perfectly circular, and have a distinctive hard center button. Unlike jellyfish that pulse through the water, Blue Buttons simply drift at the surface like living frisbees.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'buttons' and resembling jellyfish, Blue Buttons are actually more closely related to Portuguese Man o' War - they're both colonial organisms rather than single animals. The name 'Porpita' comes from a Greek word meaning 'little buckle,' another reference to their button-like appearance.
compareHints: Blue Buttons are the only species in their genus found in our waters, but they're most similar to their relative Velella (By-the-Wind Sailor). However, Velella has a distinctive triangular sail on top and is typically larger, while Blue Buttons are perfectly round and flat with no upright sail structure.
